slice: Earlier-generation Japanese MX: CRF450R 2020-2021, CRF250R 2020-2021, KX450 2020-2023, KX250 2020-2024, YZ250F 2019-2023, YZ450F 2020-2022 (setups, springs, revalves, maps, mods, issues)

records.statement: A tester baseline for the 2019-2020 tested by 160, 170 and 190 lb riders: fork 4.8 N/mm (stock 4.7), 5 mm up (stock 7), compression 12 out (stock 11), rebound 9-10 out (stock 9); shock stock 55 N/mm, 105 mm sag, high-speed 1-1/4 turns out (stock 1), low-speed 8-9 out (stock 10), rebound 9 out (stock 11). On stock fork springs run 4 mm, compression 8 out, rebound 7 out.

values.fork_alt_stock_spring: 4.7 N/mm, 4 mm, comp 8 out, reb 7 out

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - 2020 Yamaha YZ250F baseline settings

records.notes: Motocross, Southern California tracks, tester's own fast-vet pace. Article says 2020 is unchanged from 2019. The 4.8 N/mm fork spring gave better hold-up, less pitching under braking and a calmer front in ruts with only slight top-stroke firmness.

records.statement: On the 2019-2020 one tester runs the app's preloaded 'Hard Hitting' map as map 1 (a little less torque feel, more 2nd and 3rd gear pull, same engine braking) and a less-engine-braking map as map 2 (less pitching into corners, lighter mid-corner feel, slight top-end gain for a little less torque).

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - 2020 Yamaha YZ250F baseline settings

records.notes: Map grids published only as images; values not transcribed. Effects are rider feel, not dyno.

records.statement: Two of three testers kept stock 13/50 on the 2019-2020; the heavier, slower 190 lb tester preferred 13/51, which shortens 2nd and 3rd and helps riders who struggle to pull 3rd out of corners.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - 2020 Yamaha YZ250F baseline settings

records.notes: Stock engine, stock map vs tester maps.

records.topic: fixes that did and did not work 2019-2020
records.statement: On the 2019-2020 a tester found aftermarket engine mounts made the chassis less predictable and harsher on braking bumps, so kept stock. Moving the bar mounts to the forward hole facing back adds 16 mm of room for tall riders, and a 2020 YZ450F seat or firmer foam fixes the stock seat breaking down in the middle.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - 2020 Yamaha YZ250F baseline settings

records.statement: A tester's stock lithium batteries failed and left them stranded on the 2019-2020; an aftermarket battery fixed it. That hard-riding tester changed sprockets and chain about every 10 hours, clutch plates every 10-12 hours, and some high-revving riders change the timing chain about every 20 hours.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - 2020 Yamaha YZ250F baseline settings

records.notes: Intervals are one tester's practice under hard racing use, not Yamaha's schedule.

records.statement: A magazine race setup for the 2020: fork 4.7 N/mm, compression 9 out (stock 11), rebound 9 out, 5 mm up; shock 55 N/mm, 105 mm sag, high-speed 1 turn out, low-speed 10 out, rebound 8 out (stock 11). Riders under 150 lb can fit the older 4.6 N/mm fork spring; faster riders went 5-7 clicks stiffer on fork compression.

source.name: Motocross Action - MXA Race Test: 2020 Yamaha YZ250F

records.notes: Motocross, magazine test riders from novice to pro. Fork oil height can be changed in 5 cc steps. Lighter riders used more high-speed shock compression to absorb chop.

records.statement: A magazine rejected all three app presets (Hard Hitting, Linear Torque, Smooth Linear) on the 2019 and used a race-team tuner's low-to-mid map, which livened the midrange, pulled harder on top and revved further so the next gear landed in the meat of the power; with that map, 13/51 no longer forced short-shifting.

values.presets: Hard Hitting, Linear Torque, Smooth Linear
values.stock_map: all zeros, loaded in both switch positions

source.name: Motocross Action - MXA Race Test: 2019 Yamaha YZ250F

records.notes: The 2020 race test used the same map. Map values not published in text.

records.statement: Drilling two 1-1/4 inch holes in the top of the airbox cover gave the 2019-2020 a stronger top end and more over-rev; every tester liked it, the filter stayed fairly clean, but intake noise went up.

source.name: Motocross Action - MXA Race Test: 2019 Yamaha YZ250F

records.notes: Feel only, no dyno. Pair with a quality filter; the magazine said dirt ingestion was close to a concern. Repeated in the 2020 race test.

records.statement: A stainless full exhaust ($659.95 aluminium canister, $912.95 carbon) pumped up the 2019-2020's low-to-mid power without changing the top end, so testers exited corners faster and pulled through gears more smoothly.

source.name: Motocross Action - Team tested DR.D 2019 Yamaha YZ250F exhaust

records.notes: No dyno numbers published. Stock engine described as stronger above about 10,700 rpm and weaker from idle to 10,000 rpm.

records.statement: Testers found the 2019-2020 front end planted into corners (point-and-shoot), less agile than the KTM but more consistent and forgiving, balanced and straight-tracking with no setup changes; electric start added 5 lb (222 to 227 lb).

source.name: Motocross Action - MXA Race Test: 2019 Yamaha YZ250F

records.notes: Weight as reported by the magazine; fuel state not stated. Fork handles big whoops but stock spring is slightly harsh mid-stroke; shock wallows (turn rebound in).

records.statement: Testers reported a rear fender that feels like it will break when used to lift the bike, a mushy front brake from the factory (bleed after the first ride), an air filter that vibrates against the wire screen and lets dirt collect at the back of the airbox, and power that falls off about 1,000 rpm before the engine seems to want to stop.

source.name: Motocross Action - MXA Race Test: 2020 Yamaha YZ250F

records.notes: 2020 added a rubber filter grommet that helps but is not as good as aftermarket designs.

records.statement: A tester baseline for 160-190 lb riders on the 2021: fork compression 8 out, rebound 9 out, 5 mm up on fast tracks or 7 mm on tight rutted tracks; shock 104 mm sag, low-speed 8 out, high-speed 7/8 turn out, rebound 9 out.

values.fork_height: 5 mm fast tracks / 7 mm tight tracks

source.name: PulpMX - Six things about the 2021 Yamaha YZ250F

records.notes: Stock springs and valving. The 2021 felt firmer than the 2020; tester went firmer on both ends for his style. Used a tester's free-feeling map and a top-end map for more 2nd/3rd gear pull.

records.statement: A tester's 2021 baseline table for 150-180 lb riders: fork 4.7 N/mm, 4 mm, compression 8 out, rebound 9 out; shock 56 N/mm, 104 mm sag, high-speed 7/8-1 turn out, low-speed 8 out, rebound 9 out; riders over 180 lb should consider 4.8 N/mm fork springs.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - 2021 250 MX Baseline Stock Suspension Settings Bible

records.notes: The table row is labelled 'Yamaha YZ250' in the fetched text, but the article covers 250 four-strokes (it lists the KTM 250SX-F), so it is taken as the YZ250F. The 56 N/mm shock rate disagrees with the 55 N/mm quoted for 2019-2020 tests (see conflicts).

records.statement: A tester's 2023 baseline: fork 4.7 N/mm, 4 mm, compression 7 out, rebound 11 out; shock 56 N/mm, 104 mm sag, high-speed 7/8-1 turn out, low-speed 9 out, rebound 9 out, with a less-engine-braking map for chassis feel.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - 2023 250 MX Baseline Settings

records.notes: Rider weight not stated for the Yamaha row (the article's general range is 150-180 lb).

records.topic: stock vs slip-on vs full exhaust 2021
records.statement: On the 2021 a tester rated stock as snappy low-mid with short top and little over-rev; a slip-on was smoother with more mid; a full system kept most of the bottom and added mid and some top. With the spark-arrestor insert removed the full system lost bottom end, so they keep it in.

values.full_system: keeps bottom, adds mid and some top; over-rev equal to stock

source.name: PulpMX - Stock, slip-on or full system (Yamaha YZ250F/YZ450F)

records.notes: Feel only, no dyno. All runs on the tester's free-feeling Power Tuner map. Stock muffler gets raspy with hours.

records.topic: aftermarket ECU, fuel and airbox cover 2021
records.statement: On a 2021 a plug-in aftermarket ECU with a custom map, race fuel, a slip-on and a vented airbox cover ($80) gave more bottom-end pull out of corners and stronger 2nd and 3rd gear; the vented cover alone sharpened throttle response and mid pull but made more intake noise.

source.name: PulpMX - Top 5 mods 2021 Yamaha YZ250F

records.notes: Combined mods; no dyno, no separation of each part's effect.

records.statement: Testers found the 2021 cockpit small; lowering and moving the pegs back 5-10 mm helped, and the stock seat foam broke down around 20 hours.

source.name: PulpMX - Six things about the 2021 Yamaha YZ250F

records.notes: Aftermarket pegs used.

records.statement: A few owners tie hard starting, stalling and fouled plugs on 2020-2021 bikes to the idle setting (about 2,100 rpm read in the app), and one owner reported a 2019 that stopped at about 13 hours with a leaking exhaust valve, fixed under warranty.

source.name: Vital MX forum - '21 YZ250F thread (page 10)

records.notes: Small sample (2 owners on idle, 1 on the valve). Not a confirmed pattern.

records.statement: A tester baseline for roughly 170-200 lb riders on the 2020: fork 5 mm up, compression 7-8 out, rebound 8 out; shock 103 mm sag, low-speed 8 out, high-speed 3/4 turn out, rebound 8 out. If it will not lean into corners, try 102 mm sag or 7 mm fork height, not both.

values.corner_fix: 102 mm sag OR 7 mm fork height

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - 2020 Yamaha YZ450F start up/baseline settings

records.notes: Stock springs. 6 ft tester racing Southern California (won three of four holeshots in four motos on the TP 3.0 map). Stiffer, slower settings keep it planted on bigger bumps. Stock 13/49 preferred over 13/50.

records.statement: On the 2020-2021 a tester ran Yamaha's TP 3.0 preset about 80% of the time (linear, easy roll-on, pulls longer), used a softer bottom-to-mid map on soft East Coast soil (TP5 on the 2021), and found the stock map had too much bite from 0-10% throttle on hard West Coast tracks.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - 2021 Yamaha YZ450F baseline settings/mods

records.notes: Tester says these maps also work on the 2019. Also in the 2020 start-up article (?p=13243).

records.statement: A magazine race setup for the 2020: fork 5.0 N/mm, compression 9 out (stock 8), rebound 8 out (stock 10), 5 mm up; shock 58 N/mm, 105 mm sag (stock 100), low-speed 12 out, rebound 11 out. The stiff shock spring still gave usable sag for riders down to 150 lb.

values.shock_hsc: printed as '10 turns out' (likely clicks; unclear)

source.name: Motocross Action - The real 2020 450 four-stroke shootout

records.notes: Motocross, magazine riders vet to pro. One Kayaba SSS fork click is worth a couple of clicks on other brands. Magazine also measured 238 lb without fuel, 247 lb with fuel.

records.statement: In one 2020 shootout all seven testers, from a 150 lb former pro to a 240 lb vet pro, ranked the YZ450F first or second; a 215 lb C vet went two fork clicks softer, and a 160 lb vet pro used the TP map and added a couple of rebound clicks to calm a busy front end.

values.testers: 150-240 lb, C vet to current pro

source.name: Vital MX - 2020 Vital MX 450 Shootout full test

records.notes: Sag not reported.

records.statement: A revalve on stock springs gave the 2020-2021 fork more hold-up and less diving off throttle without deflecting on braking bumps, and a firmer shock that squatted less under acceleration; spring-tube inserts added mid-stroke firmness.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - 2021 Yamaha YZ450F baseline settings/mods

records.notes: Rider 165-195 lb range. Stock fork dives off throttle and upsets the shock on corner entry. Same tester's baseline on stock valving: 5 mm, comp 6-7, reb 7-8; 104 mm sag, LSC 8, HSC 3/4, reb 7-8.

records.statement: A tester baseline for 165-195 lb riders on the 2022 (new valving, so 2021 settings no longer apply): fork 3 mm, compression 7 out, rebound 9-10 out; shock 104 mm sag, low-speed 8 out, high-speed 7/8 turn out, rebound 10-11 out; if it still won't corner, try 102 mm sag or 5 mm fork height.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - 2022 Yamaha YZ450F baseline settings/tips

records.notes: Maps: a 'magic' preset for soft East Coast soil, TP 3.0 as default. Stock 13/49 preferred. Fork slightly soft under hard braking until broken in.

records.statement: The same tester's later 2022 table for 160-195 lb riders: fork 4 mm, compression 10 out, rebound 8 out; shock 104 mm sag, low-speed 10 out, high-speed 1 turn out, rebound 13 out, backing off high-speed slightly lets the rear squat more out of corners.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - 2022 450 MX Baseline Settings

records.notes: Differs from the September 2021 article (see conflicts); settled after more hours.

records.statement: On the 2021 a tester found stock strong but too responsive low with the TP 3 map; slip-ons either smoothed the hit but lost mid and 3rd-gear pull, or kept the bite and smoothed 20-30% throttle; full systems smoothed roll-on and added mid and top pull, and the quietest one gave the best hard-pack traction.

records.notes: Feel only; three brands compared, no dyno.

records.statement: On one magazine's in-house dyno the 2021 made 53.1 hp at 9,700 rpm and 32.7 lb-ft at 7,400 rpm, less than the Honda, Husqvarna and KTM from 6,400 rpm to peak, with the strongest bottom-to-mid hit of the group.

source.name: Dirt Rider - 2021 Yamaha YZ450F dyno test

records.notes: In-house dyno, type not named; map and fuel not stated. Another magazine lists 58.56 hp @ 9,700 / 34.36 lb-ft for the 2021 (see conflicts). Do not compare across dynos.

records.statement: A tester says the 2020-2022 does not need aftermarket triple clamps; a softer-terrain front tyre in place of the stock one improves initial lean into corners.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - 2022 Yamaha YZ450F baseline settings/tips

records.statement: A magazine race setup for the 2021: fork 5.0 N/mm, compression 10 clicks, rebound 15 out, flush; shock 56 N/mm (stock 54), 107 mm sag, low-speed 12 out, high-speed 2 turns out, rebound 8 out. Riders under 150 lb can keep the 54 N/mm shock spring.

source.name: Motocross Action - MXA Race Test: 2021 Honda CRF450

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - 2020 Honda CRF450R start up/baseline settings

records.notes: Stock springs.

records.topic: ECU, muffler, filter and pivot-bolt mods 2020
records.statement: On the 2020 a plug-in aftermarket ECU gave more, longer and smoother power with better over-rev; a full muffler smoothed 0-15% throttle and saved about 1.5 lb; removing the filter screen (keeping the cage) added mid response; and re-torquing the swingarm pivot from 65 to 60 ft-lb added rear traction.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - 2020 Honda CRF450R start up/baseline settings

records.notes: Feel only, no dyno. Tester notes stock maps 1 and 3 have jerky roll-on through corners. 13/48 for a stock bike conflicts with the 13/49 stock gearing quoted elsewhere.

records.statement: Water in the handlebar map switch can stop the 2020 from starting (wrap it before washing), and one tester changes oil every 2-3 engine hours because it darkens quickly.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - 2020 Honda CRF450R start up/baseline settings

source.name: Vital MX - 2020 Vital MX 450 Shootout full test

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - 2021 250 MX Baseline Stock Suspension Settings Bible

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - Yoshimura RS-9T stainless full system (2020 CRF250R)

records.notes: Keep OEM pivot torque if the rear feels planted on chop.

source.name: Motocross Action - Ask the MXperts: best 2020 Kawasaki KX250 spring rates

records.notes: Stiff stock forks did not bother them on smooth tracks with big jumps.

records.statement: A tester baseline for the 2020 from 150-190 lb novice-to-pro riders: fork compression 12 out, rebound 9 out, 5 mm; shock low-speed 5 out, high-speed 1-1/4 turns out, rebound 15 out, 103-104 mm sag, to stop the shock riding low under acceleration.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - 2020 Kawasaki KX250 baseline/start up settings

records.notes: Article calls the suspension KYB; the 2020 KX250 used Showa per other sources (see conflicts). Stock springs.

records.statement: On the 2020 a tester found the green coupler the most usable overall; the white helped slower or weaker-cornering riders with low-end recovery but fell off earlier on top; the black suited hard-pack or loose tracks and newer riders with better rear hook-up and less rpm response. Heavier, slower riders ran 13/51 with green plus a custom map.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - 2020 Kawasaki KX250 baseline/start up settings

records.notes: Conflicts with a magazine that calls white aggressive and preferred by pros (tg-055).

records.statement: A magazine race setup for the 2021-2022: fork 4.9 N/mm, compression 8 out (stock 12), rebound 12 out (stock 11), standard height, 5-10 cc oil removed; shock 54 N/mm, 103 mm sag (preferred to 105), high-speed 1-1/2 turns out, low-speed 10 out, rebound 13 out (stock 15); 52T rear sprocket.

source.name: Motocross Action - MXA Race Test: 2021 Kawasaki KX250

records.notes: Softer fork settings let it drop into the harsh mid-stroke, so testers went stiffer; revalve recommended. Two clicks more rebound stopped the rear kicking at 103 mm. 2022 test repeats the setup.

records.statement: A factory tuner's custom map for the 2021-2022, built with the $699.95 calibration kit, uses the aggressive coupler's ignition with the mellow coupler's fuel; testers found more midrange and longer pull into the upper rpm, noticeable but not huge.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - 2022 Kawasaki KX250 review/suspension settings

records.notes: Magazine reports describe the black coupler as most aggressive low-end and the white as most aggressive mid-top (see conflicts); kx-066 also covers the mixed map.

records.statement: A tester's 2021-2022 baselines: 150-170 lb riders use the 4.9 N/mm fork at 4 mm, compression 11-12 out, rebound 10 out, and a 54 N/mm shock at 103 mm sag, high-speed 1-1/4, low-speed 8, rebound 10; 175-200 lb riders keep 4.9 fork at compression 9-10, rebound 12, and fit a 56 N/mm shock at 104 mm, high-speed 1-1/2, low-speed 11, rebound 9.

values.150-170 lb: fork 4.9, 4 mm, C 11-12, R 10; shock 54, 103 mm, HSC 1-1/4, LSC 8, R 10
values.175-200 lb: fork 4.9, 4 mm, C 9-10, R 12; shock 56, 104 mm, HSC 1-1/2, LSC 11, R 9

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - 2022 Kawasaki KX250 review/suspension settings

records.notes: 2022 unchanged from 2021. Heavier band oddly runs softer fork compression with stiffer shock.

records.statement: A tester's 2021 and 2023 tables give the same baseline for 150-180 lb: fork 4.9 N/mm, 4 mm, compression 9 out, rebound 10 out; shock 54 N/mm, 102-103 mm sag, high-speed 1-1/4 turns out, low-speed 9 out, rebound 11 out; over 180 lb fit 5.0 N/mm fork and 56 N/mm shock springs and soften compression two clicks each end.

source.name: Keefer Inc. Tested - 2021 250 MX Baseline Stock Suspension Settings Bible

records.notes: Identical row repeated in the 2023 250 baseline (https://www.keeferinctesting.com/?p=24087).

records.statement: A magazine's 2023 setup: fork 4.7 N/mm (stock 4.9), compression 12 out, rebound 12 out, 5 mm, oil cut from 290 cc toward 260 cc (still stiff); shock 54 N/mm, 100 mm sag (stock 103), low-speed 12 out, high-speed 1-7/8 turns out (stock 1-1/2), rebound 13 out (stock 15); white coupler and 51T rear.

source.name: Motocross Action - MXA Race Test: 2023 Kawasaki KX250

records.notes: Aim to finish about 1-1/2 in from bottoming (zip tie). 100 mm sag sharpened turning; 105 mm pulled weight off the front. A 155 lb tester strapped two 2.5 lb weights to the front frame rails for front grip (temporary fix). Revalve recommended.

records.statement: One magazine measured the 2023 at 44.66 hp, just behind the FC250 (44.76) and 250SX-F (45.22); its initial response was detuned versus 2022, so bottom snap is weaker, but midrange and top are clearly stronger.

source.name: Motocross Action - MXA Race Test: 2023 Kawasaki KX250

records.notes: Dyno type and rpm not stated. 2023 changes: narrower intake valve angle, 14.1:1 piston, 100 mm longer head pipe, heavier rotor, advanced timing.

records.statement: On one magazine's dyno the 2021-2022 trailed the top 250s by more than 2 hp below about 9,000 rpm, led from about 9,500 to 13,700 rpm, and missed the FC250's peak by 0.12 hp; the 2021 engine changes cut the low-mid gap from 4 hp to 2 hp.

source.name: Motocross Action - MXA Race Test: 2022 Kawasaki KX250

records.notes: Dyno type not stated; peak value not printed.

records.statement: Testers found the 2021-2023 stable in a straight line but pushing in flat or off-camber corners because the 250 engine sits far back in the 450 frame; raising the forks in the clamps made it worse, while sitting forward, softer fork springs, less sag (100 mm) or extra weight on the front frame rails helped.

source.name: Motocross Action - MXA Race Test: 2022 Kawasaki KX250

records.notes: Also in the 2021 and 2023 race tests.

records.statement: On the 2021-2023 the stock front chain roller wears in about 5 hours and can come apart around 10 hours, and the chain guide is worn by about 15 hours; aftermarket parts fix both.

source.name: Motocross Action - MXA Race Test: 2021 Kawasaki KX250

records.notes: Repeated in 2022 and 2023 tests.
